growth_story.headline: Luxembourg's finance-led boom ended in 2008; output has since grown with the workforce, but income per person is back near its 2006 level.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2007 income per person grew 3.3 percent a year, as Luxembourg's financial sector became a leading international hub for investment funds and a key contributor to growth. The 2008 global financial crisis hit through the banks, many of them subsidiaries of foreign groups: income per person fell 2.1 percent in 2008 and 5.0 percent in 2009, and the era from 2008 to 2025 has averaged -0.4 percent a year. Over that second era, the sources say, output grew mainly because the workforce grew, with immigrants and cross-border workers, while labour productivity stalled. After a rebound of 5.3 percent in 2021, rising interest rates in 2022 and 2023 hit the financial sector and ended a long housing boom, and income per person fell every year from 2022 to 2025. Income per person peaked in 2007, is now 8.1 percent below that peak and about where it first was in 2006; growth averaged -0.2 percent a year over 2016 to 2025, against 0.5 in the decade before.

threads.title: Finance builds the boom
threads.text: From 1990 to 2007 Luxembourg grew into a leading centre for asset management and investment funds. The OECD calls this financial sector a key contributor to growth in that era, when income per person rose 3.3 percent a year.

threads.title: The 2008 crisis hits banks
threads.text: Growth came to a sudden halt in the third quarter of 2008, and some of Luxembourg's bank subsidiaries had to raise cash for their foreign parent groups. Since the crisis the financial sector's share of the economy has fallen. Income per person dropped 5.0 percent in 2009 and has not regained its 2007 peak.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe an economy whose output kept growing after 2008, carried by a fast-rising workforce, and the IMF reports positive growth in 2025. The data tell a flatter story: income per person has averaged -0.4 percent a year since 2008, fell every year from 2022 to 2025, and is about where it first was in 2006. Output has grown, but mostly by adding workers rather than by raising output per worker, so little of that growth shows up as higher income per person.
